domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: Evaluation is identified as the number one pain point in AI engineering, and the talk discusses evaluation practices including offline eval and human review as measurement methods. The talk is a cross-cutting industry survey not tied to any specific application vertical. The talk covers production deployment practices alongside the evaluation and monitoring of deployed AI systems. The talk presents survey findings in an accessible format without requiring deep technical prerequisites. This is a conference presentation delivering early findings from an industry survey. Findings are based on self-reported survey data from 500 respondents, which may not be fully representative.

summary: Barr Yaron presents early findings from the 2025 State of AI Engineering survey, which gathered 500 respondents including many conference attendees. The survey reveals that while the largest group identifies as engineers, titles remain varied and the AI engineer label is still gaining ground. Notably, many veteran software engineers with 10+ years of experience are AI newcomers, with nearly half having worked with AI for three years or less. More than half of respondents use LLMs for both internal and external use cases, with OpenAI models dominating external-facing products. Top use cases include code generation, code intelligence, and content generation, with 94% of LLM users deploying across at least two use cases. RAG is the most popular customization method at 70%, and fine-tuning is more prevalent than expected, with LoRA/QLoRA mentioned by 40% of fine-tuners and supervised fine-tuning being the most popular core approach. Over 50% update models at least monthly, 17% weekly, while 70% update prompts at least monthly and 10% daily. Despite this, 31% have no prompt management system. A significant multimodal production gap exists, with image, video, and audio lagging far behind text usage, though audio shows the highest intent for future adoption at 37%. Agents are defined as systems where an LLM controls core decision-making. While 80% say LLMs work well at work, less than 20% say the same about agents, though fewer than 1 in 10 say they will never use agents. Most production agents have write access with human-in-the-loop oversight. For monitoring, 60% use standard observability and 50%+ rely on offline eval, with human review remaining the most popular evaluation method. 65% use dedicated vector databases, with 35% self-hosting and 30% using third-party providers. On opinions, most respondents believe agents should disclose they are AI, would pay more for inference-time compute, believe transformers will dominate in 2030, and think open and closed source models will converge. The mean estimate for US Gen Z having AI romantic partners is 26%. Evaluation is cited as the most painful aspect of AI engineering. The talk concludes with top 10 podcast and newsletter recommendations.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Background
sections.summary: Barr Yaron introduces herself as an investment partner at Amplify Partners investing in technical founders, and announces the presentation of early findings from the 2025 State of AI Engineering survey.

sections.title: Survey Sample and Demographics
sections.summary: The survey had 500 respondents, with the largest group identifying as engineers. Titles are varied despite the AI engineering conference context, and the AI engineer label is gaining ground. Many veteran software engineers with 10+ years experience are AI newcomers, with nearly half having worked with AI for 3 years or less.

sections.title: LLM Usage and Use Cases
sections.summary: More than half of respondents use LLMs for both internal and external use cases. OpenAI models dominate external-facing products, with 3 of top 5 and half of top 10 models from OpenAI. Top use cases are code generation, code intelligence, and content generation. 94% of LLM users deploy at least 2 use cases and 82% at least 3, showing strong heterogeneity.

sections.title: Customization: RAG and Fine-Tuning
sections.summary: RAG is the most popular customization method at 70%. Fine-tuning is more prevalent than expected, especially among researchers and research engineers. 40% of fine-tuners use LoRA or QLoRA, reflecting preference for parameter-efficient methods. DPO, reinforcement fine-tuning, and supervised fine-tuning (most popular core approach) are also used, along with hybrid approaches.

sections.title: Model and Prompt Update Cadence
sections.summary: Over 50% update models at least monthly, 17% weekly. 70% update prompts at least monthly and 1 in 10 daily. Despite this frequency, 31% have no way of managing prompts.

sections.title: Multimodal Production Gap
sections.summary: Image, video, and audio usage all significantly lag text usage, termed the 'multimodal production gap.' Audio has the highest intent to adopt among non-users at 37%, signaling a coming audio wave.

sections.title: Agents: Adoption and Capabilities
sections.summary: Agents are defined as systems where an LLM controls core decision-making. 80% say LLMs work well at work but less than 20% say the same about agents. Fewer than 1 in 10 say they will never use agents. Most production agents have write access, typically with human-in-the-loop oversight.

sections.title: Monitoring, Observability, and Storage
sections.summary: 60% use standard observability and 50%+ rely on offline eval. Human review remains the most popular evaluation method. Most respondents rely on internal metrics for model usage monitoring. 65% use dedicated vector databases, with 35% self-hosting and 30% using third-party providers.

sections.title: Other Fun Stuff: Opinions and Predictions
sections.summary: Most respondents believe agents should disclose being AI, would pay more for inference-time compute (but not by a wide margin), believe transformers will dominate in 2030, and think open and closed source models will converge. Mean estimate for US Gen Z having AI romantic partners is 26%. Evaluation is the top pain point in AI engineering.

sections.title: Content Recommendations and Conclusion
sections.summary: Top 10 podcasts and newsletters for AI engineering learning are shared, with Swix's Latent Space appearing on both lists. A full report with more details including favorite models and tools is promised for the following week.
